title: The Room Will Not Stop
subtitle: Two days of spinning, from the emergency department to the rehabilitation plan
description: Recognizing acute vestibular syndrome, the bedside HINTS examination, why hearing is checked, making the diagnosis, deciding which side, and what to do now and later.

steps.title: Step 1/6: What Kind of Dizzy
steps.scenario:
A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife. Two days ago he woke with the room spinning. It has not stopped. He has vomited several times, cannot walk without holding the wall, and every head movement makes it worse. He has no headache, no hearing change, no ringing, no weakness or numbness, no double vision. He had a cold last week.

He says the world moves; he does not feel faint.
steps.question: How do you classify his presentation?

options.text: (A) Presyncope
(B) Acute vestibular syndrome
(C) Episodic vestibular syndrome
(D) Chronic vestibular syndrome

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: B

The first job with a dizzy patient is to sort the word. Vertigo is an illusion of motion: the room spins, or the ground tilts, or the world bounces with each step, which is oscillopsia. Dizziness that is lightheadedness or a feeling of fainting is presyncope, and it belongs to the heart and the circulation, not the ear. His is vertigo.

The second job is the time course. Acute vestibular syndrome is vertigo of sudden onset that is continuous for days, with nausea, vomiting, unsteadiness, intolerance of head movement and nystagmus. That is him. It has two main causes, vestibular neuritis and posterior circulation stroke, and the whole point of the examination in Step 2 is to tell them apart. Episodic vestibular syndrome is attacks that come and go with normal periods between, minutes to hours each: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, Meniere's disease, vestibular migraine. Chronic vestibular syndrome is weeks to months of imbalance without discrete attacks.

Why the others fail:
(A) He does not feel faint. He feels the world move. Presyncope does not cause nystagmus or vomiting with head turning.
(C) Episodes have gaps. He has had two days without one.
(D) Two days is not chronic, and chronic syndromes do not start with vomiting.

Keypoint: vertigo means the world moves; continuous for days with nausea and unsteadiness is acute vestibular syndrome, and the next question is neuritis or stroke.

Reference: Strupp M, Bisdorff A, Furman J, et al. Acute unilateral vestibulopathy/vestibular neuritis: diagnostic criteria. Consensus document of the Committee for the Classification of Vestibular Disorders of the Barany Society. J Vestib Res. 2022;32(5):389-406.

steps.title: Step 2/6: Three Things at the Bedside
steps.scenario:
You examine his eyes.

    Nystagmus       Horizontal with a torsional component, fast phase to the left in primary gaze. Stronger when he looks left, weaker but still left-beating when he looks right. Reduced when he fixates on your finger.
    Head impulse    You turn his head quickly to the right: his eyes slip with the head and a corrective saccade brings them back to your nose. To the left: eyes stay fixed on your nose.
    Skew            Cover one eye, then the other: no vertical correction.
steps.media: Load video: Nystagmus under Frenzel goggles from your own patient, 10 seconds, muted, de-identified: left-beating horizontal nystagmus increasing on left gaze. Caption: 'Nystagmus, primary and left gaze.'
steps.question: What does the HINTS examination show?

options.text: (A) A central pattern; he needs an urgent MRI before anything else
(B) The findings are contradictory and cannot be interpreted
(C) A normal examination; the vertigo is not vestibular
(D) A peripheral pattern: abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus that follows Alexander's law, no skew

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

HINTS is three bedside tests, and all three point the same way here.

Head impulse. A quick passive head turn tests the vestibulo-ocular reflex on that side. If the labyrinth or nerve is working, the eyes stay locked on the target. If it is not, the eyes go with the head and a catch-up saccade brings them back. His catch-up saccade is on rightward turns. That is a peripheral sign, and it says the right side is weak. A normal head impulse in a patient with acute vestibular syndrome is the dangerous result, because it means the vestibular periphery is intact and the cause is central.

Nystagmus. Peripheral nystagmus beats one way, away from the weak side, and it obeys Alexander's law: it is strongest when he looks in the direction of the fast phase, weaker when he looks the other way, but it never reverses. It is suppressed by visual fixation, which is why you look under Frenzel goggles. His is left-beating in every gaze position, stronger on left gaze, damped by fixation. Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or is purely vertical or purely torsional, is central.

Skew. A vertical misalignment of the eyes on cover testing is a brainstem sign. He has none.

Abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus, no skew: this is the benign combination. In the original study HINTS identified stroke in acute vestibular syndrome more accurately than early MRI, which misses a proportion of posterior fossa infarcts in the first 48 hours. The examination is not a reason to skip imaging when the pattern is central; it is a reason not to be reassured by a normal early MRI.

Why the others fail:
(A) The central pattern is the opposite of what you found: a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or a skew. He has an abnormal head impulse and none of the other two.
(B) The three findings agree with each other and with Alexander's law. Nothing is contradictory.
(C) Spontaneous nystagmus and a catch-up saccade are not normal. They are the examination of a damaged vestibular periphery.

Keypoint: catch-up saccade on head turn, nystagmus that beats one way and grows toward its fast phase, no skew: peripheral. A normal head impulse in acute vestibular syndrome is the finding that means stroke.

Reference: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.

steps.title: Step 3/6: The Tuning Fork
steps.scenario:
Before you leave the bedside you take out a 512 Hz tuning fork.

    Weber    Midline
    Rinne    Air conduction louder than bone, both ears

A pure-tone audiogram the next morning is normal and symmetric.
steps.media: Load image: Pure-tone audiogram from your own patient, de-identified: normal symmetric thresholds. Caption: 'Audiogram.'
steps.question: Why did you check his hearing, and what does a normal result tell you?

options.text: (A) To separate the labyrinth from the nerve: normal hearing means the cochlea is spared, which points to the vestibular nerve rather than the whole labyrinth
(B) Normal hearing rules out any inner ear cause and makes the vertigo central
(C) Hearing is unrelated to vertigo; the fork test was unnecessary
(D) Normal hearing today excludes Meniere's disease permanently

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The cochlea and the vestibular labyrinth share a bony capsule, a blood supply and, for part of their course, a nerve. A process that hits the whole inner ear takes hearing with it: labyrinthitis, a labyrinthine infarct, a first attack of Meniere's disease. A process confined to the vestibular nerve leaves hearing alone. So a tuning fork at the bedside, confirmed by an audiogram, is the quickest way to ask which of those you are dealing with. His hearing is normal on both sides. The cochlea is spared. What is damaged is the vestibular nerve, or the vestibular labyrinth alone, and either way it is the vestibular system without the cochlea.

The next tests add detail rather than change the diagnosis. Caloric testing shows a reduced response on the weak side. Video head impulse testing measures the vestibulo-ocular reflex gain for each canal and records the catch-up saccades you saw with your hands. Vestibular evoked myogenic potentials tell you whether the superior division, the inferior division, or both are involved. They are ordered once he can tolerate them, not in the emergency department.

Why the others fail:
(B) Normal hearing does not make vertigo central. Vestibular neuritis, the commonest peripheral cause of acute vestibular syndrome, has normal hearing by definition.
(C) Hearing is how you tell neuritis from labyrinthitis at the bedside. The fork takes thirty seconds and changes the diagnosis.
(D) Meniere's disease is diagnosed on a documented low-frequency hearing loss during attacks over time. One normal audiogram on one day does not exclude it, though it makes a first Meniere's attack unlikely here, and a two-day continuous course does not fit Meniere's anyway.

Keypoint: check hearing in every acute vertigo; spared hearing means the nerve, lost hearing means the whole labyrinth.

Reference: Strupp M, Bisdorff A, Furman J, et al. J Vestib Res. 2022;32(5):389-406.

steps.title: Step 4/6: The Diagnosis
steps.scenario: Two days of continuous spinning vertigo with nausea and unsteadiness. Left-beating unidirectional nystagmus, abnormal head impulse to the right, no skew. Normal hearing. No headache, no neurological signs. A cold the week before.
steps.question: What is the diagnosis?

options.text: (A) Meniere's disease
(B) Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
(C) Labyrinthitis
(D) Vestibular neuritis

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: D

Vestibular neuritis is an acute, sustained loss of function of one vestibular nerve, usually the superior division, with the cochlea spared. The picture is the one he has: continuous vertigo for days, nausea and vomiting, unsteadiness toward the weak side, a spontaneous unidirectional nystagmus that obeys Alexander's law, an abnormal head impulse on the weak side, normal hearing, and no central signs. A viral illness in the preceding weeks is common. The diagnostic criteria are clinical; the vHIT and caloric confirm the side and the severity but the diagnosis is made at the bedside.

Why the others fail:
(A) Meniere's disease is episodic: attacks of vertigo lasting minutes to hours, with fluctuating low-frequency hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness, and normal periods between. Two days of continuous vertigo with normal hearing is not a Meniere's attack.
(B) Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is brief, seconds to a minute, provoked by specific head positions, with no spontaneous nystagmus at rest. He has spontaneous nystagmus and continuous vertigo. The Dix-Hallpike is still worth doing once he can tolerate it, because BPPV can follow neuritis, but it is not the diagnosis today.
(C) Labyrinthitis is the same acute vestibular picture plus hearing loss, because the whole labyrinth is inflamed. His hearing is normal. That is the one finding that separates the two, and it is why Step 3 mattered.

Keypoint: continuous vertigo for days, peripheral HINTS, and normal hearing is vestibular neuritis; add hearing loss and it is labyrinthitis; make it episodic and it is Meniere's or BPPV.

Reference: Strupp M, Bisdorff A, Furman J, et al. Acute unilateral vestibulopathy/vestibular neuritis: diagnostic criteria. J Vestib Res. 2022;32(5):389-406.

steps.title: Step 5/6: Which Side
steps.scenario:
Day four. He can sit up. The vestibular laboratory reports:

    Caloric      Right canal paresis 68 percent
    vHIT         Right lateral canal gain 0.45 with overt and covert saccades; left canals normal
    cVEMP        Present bilaterally, symmetric
    oVEMP        Absent on the right
steps.media: Load image: vHIT printout from your own patient, de-identified: reduced right lateral canal gain with saccades, normal left. Caption: 'Video head impulse test.'
steps.question: Which side is affected, and which findings tell you?

options.text: (A) Left, because the nystagmus beats to the left
(B) Cannot be determined without MRI
(C) Right: the nystagmus beats away from it, the head impulse is abnormal toward it, the caloric is weak on it, and the absent right oVEMP points to the superior vestibular nerve
(D) Both sides, because the caloric asymmetry is under 100 percent

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: C

Every finding points right, and it is worth knowing why each one does.

Nystagmus beats away from the weak side. The two labyrinths push the eyes in opposite directions and normally cancel. Lose the right, and the intact left pushes the eyes slowly to the right; the fast phase, which is the corrective jerk and the one we name, goes left. Left-beating nystagmus means a right lesion.

Head impulse is abnormal toward the weak side. Turning the head right tests the right lateral canal. His catch-up saccade was on rightward turns.

Caloric is weak on the weak side. Irrigating the right ear produced 68 percent less response than the left; anything over about 25 percent asymmetry is significant.

VEMPs say which part of the nerve. The ocular VEMP tests the utricle and superior vestibular nerve; the cervical VEMP tests the saccule and inferior vestibular nerve. His oVEMP is absent on the right and his cVEMP is normal. This is superior vestibular neuritis, the commonest pattern: the superior division supplies the lateral and anterior canals and the utricle, and it runs through a longer, narrower bony channel than the inferior division, which is thought to be why it is more often affected.

Why the others fail:
(A) The commonest error. The fast phase is the correction, not the lesion. It beats away from the damaged side.
(B) The side is written all over the bedside examination and the laboratory. MRI has no part in localizing a peripheral lesion.
(D) A canal paresis is expressed as an asymmetry between the two ears. Sixty-eight percent is a large unilateral deficit, not a bilateral one; bilateral loss would show reduced responses on both sides and no asymmetry.

Keypoint: nystagmus beats away, head impulse fails toward, caloric is weak on the affected side; VEMPs tell you superior or inferior division.

Reference: Strupp M, Bisdorff A, Furman J, et al. J Vestib Res. 2022;32(5):389-406.

steps.title: Step 6/6: Now and Later
steps.scenario:
Right superior vestibular neuritis. Day four, sitting up, still nauseated with head movement, walking with a hand on the wall.

He asks what happens now, and whether he will get better.
steps.question: What do you do now, and what do you plan for later?

options.text: (A) Supportive care for about a week: antiemetic and a vestibular suppressant for the first few days only, then off; get him up and moving; at review, assess whether he is compensating and start vestibular rehabilitation
(B) A course of oral steroid; rehabilitation is not needed because the nerve will recover on its own
(C) Start vestibular rehabilitation today and give a vestibular suppressant to take as needed for the next month
(D) Bed rest with regular vestibular suppressants until the vertigo has fully stopped

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Recovery from vestibular neuritis is mostly not the nerve recovering. It is the brain recalibrating to a permanently weaker signal from one side, which is central compensation, and compensation is driven by movement. Every head turn that provokes a moment of vertigo is the brain being shown the mismatch it needs to correct. So the plan has two phases.

Now, for the first few days: control the nausea so he can eat and drink, and use a vestibular suppressant such as diphenidol or a benzodiazepine for no more than about three days, because beyond that it blunts the very error signal the brain is trying to learn from. Get him out of bed as soon as he can stand. Steroids are debated: a randomized trial found methylprednisolone improved caloric recovery at one year but the clinical benefit is uncertain, and the consensus is that they may be considered rather than required.

Later, at the one-week review: look at whether he is compensating. Spontaneous nystagmus fading, walking without support, tolerating head turns. If he is compensating on his own, encourage activity and review again. If he is not, or if he is anxious and avoiding movement, refer for vestibular rehabilitation: a structured program of gaze stabilization and balance exercises with a therapist, which shortens the time to recovery and reduces the chance of chronic dizziness.

Why the others fail:
(B) Steroids are at most an option, not the plan, and they do nothing for compensation. Leaving out rehabilitation is the mistake that turns a two-week illness into a six-month one in the patients who do not compensate on their own.
(C) Rehabilitation on day four is fine in principle, but a suppressant taken as needed for a month undoes it. Every dose delays compensation. Suppressants are for the first days, then stopped.
(D) Bed rest is the worst thing for him. The vertigo does not stop because the nerve heals; it stops because the brain adapts, and it cannot adapt lying still.

Keypoint: suppressants for days, not weeks; move early; at one week decide whether he is compensating and send him to rehabilitation if he is not.

Reference: Strupp M, Zingler VC, Arbusow V, et al. Methylprednisolone, valacyclovir, or the combination for vestibular neuritis. N Engl J Med. 2004;351(4):354-361. Hall CD, Herdman SJ, Whitney SL, et al. Vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction: an updated clinical practice guideline from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association. J Neurol Phys Ther. 2022;46(2):118-177. Strupp M, Bisdorff A, Furman J, et al. J Vestib Res. 2022;32(5):389-406.
